Article Title: 'This is treason': Rahul Gandhi revives 'vote chori' charge after report of rift within EC
Article Text:
EC rejects reports of differences

NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Wednesday revived his "vote chori" charge against the Election Commission and accused election officials of committing "treason".In a post on X, Rahul said, "I am telling the EC and election officials clearly: What you are doing is wrong. This is treason, this is against the country. Do not forget that. The time will come when we will catch you. You will not be able to escape."His remarks came after an Indian Express report claimed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections to the poll panel's actions at least 14 times over the past 10 months during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The report said the commissioners had flagged issues relating to the addition and deletion of voters as well as the handling of voter data.Senior Congress leaders KC Venugopal and P Chidambaram also stepped up their attack on the poll panel following the report.Chidambaram said the opposition had already contended that several decisions concerning the SIR were wrong and questioned how Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's view could become the decision of the Commission if the two Election Commissioners had taken a contrary position."The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that if the decision-making process is flawed or wrong, the decision will also be flawed or wrong. The opposition has contended that many decisions concerning SIR were wrong. Now, it is revealed that the decision-making process was also wrong," Chidambaram said."If two ECs have taken a contrary view, how could the CEC make his view the 'decision' of the ECI? All decisions of the ECI in recent years should be reviewed by a Parliamentary Committee. Meanwhile, the SIR process should be suspended immediately all over the country," he added.Congress general secretary KC Venugopal also targeted CEC Gyanesh Kumar and demanded his removal."There is no doubt remaining. Mr Gyanesh Kumar has no right to remain in office. How the hell can one man, acting on His Master's orders, strike off names at whim? How can he sideline fellow Constitutional officers to only take blatantly illegal steps that put our democracy in danger?" Venugopal said."The right to vote is an essential Constitutional power given to every citizen, the fundamental bedrock of our democracy. If it is to be taken away, due process must be followed with utmost probity," he added.The Election Commission, however, rejected reports of differences within the poll panel over the SIR and said all decisions related to the exercise were taken unanimously.Officials told news agency PTI that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi did raise concerns over some aspects of voter roll deletion and database handling, but these did not amount to disagreement with the final decisions taken by the Commission.EC sources said all decisions of the Commission, including those relating to the SIR, had the approval of Sandhu, Joshi and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Officials also pointed out that the law governing the Election Commission, as well as a Supreme Court judgment, provides that decisions should, as far as possible, be taken unanimously. Where unanimity is not possible, the majority view prevails.
Article Summary: Ec rejects reports of differences over the special intensive revision (sir) of electoral rolls. Rahul gandhi accuses election officials of committing "treason" congress leaders kc venugopal and p chidambaram also step up their attack on the poll panel.

NEW DELHI: The Election Commission has rejected reports of differences within the poll panel over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), saying all decisions related to the exercise were taken "unanimously".The poll body clarified that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi did raise concerns over some aspects of voter roll deletion and database handling, but these did not amount to disagreement with the final decisions taken by the Commission.The clarification came after an Indian Express report triggered a row by claiming that the two Election Commissioners had raised objections to the Commission's decisions 14 times over the past 10 months during the SIR exercise.EC sources told PTI that all decisions taken by the Election Commission, including those related to the SIR, were unanimous and had the approval of Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi as well as Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Responding to queries, officials said Sandhu and Joshi had flagged issues related to the deletion of names from electoral rolls in various states and the handling of voter data.Officials also pointed out that the law governing the Election Commission, as well as a Supreme Court judgment, provides that decisions should, as far as possible, be taken unanimously. Where unanimity is not possible, the majority view prevails.Meanwhile, opposition sharpened its attack on the Election Commission over the SIR, claiming it was meant to target electors not aligned to the BJP and its allies.Urging the Supreme Court to take suo motu cognizance of the issue, several opposition parties attacked Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and accused him of becoming a puppet of those in power.In a social media post, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav accused the poll panel of hatching a conspiracy to "wipe out democracy.""This is an extremely serious news that in the past 10 months, 2 Election Commissioners have registered their objections 14 times against the Election Commission's wrong decisions," Akhilesh said."This directly means that all Election Commissioners are not able to perform their rightful duties. If the members of an independent body do not have the freedom to carry out just actions or if there is no hearing of theirs, then these are extremely fatal and dangerous circumstances for democracy. For some people to betray democracy by becoming puppets of those in power is a grave constitutional crime. This is nothing less than a conspiracy to wipe out democracy," he added.Mamata Trinamool Congress (MTMC) also slammed CEC Kumar and said that the opposition should reintroduce the impeachment motion against Kumar in Parliament."Five months ago, more than 60 Rajya Sabha Members of Parliament... when only 50 were needed, wrote to the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha moving a motion to remove the Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, that was five months ago. Now today, after this big news break that two Election Commissioners objected to many of the CEC's actions, it's time to bring out the Rajya Sabha motion to impeach the CEC and save democracy," MTMC's Derek O' O'Brien said.The issue is likely to escalate further as leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi has been vehement in his criticism of the Election Commission and the SIR process, alleging that it has resulted in the denial of voting rights.
Article Summary: The election commission has rejected reports of differences within the poll panel over the special intensive revision (sir) the poll body said all decisions related to the exercise were taken "unanimously" election commissioners sukhbir singh sandhu and vivek joshi raised concerns over some aspects of voter roll deletion and database handling.

Article Title: PM Modi likely to visit Canada in December to lock in trade deal: Canadian PM Carney
Article Text:
PM Modi and Canadian PM Mark Carney (File photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to visit Canada in December to seal the trade deal between New Delhi and Ottawa, Canadian PM Mark Carney said on Tuesday.Speaking on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, Carney said that the relationship between India and Canada is "exceptionally important" and claimed that both countries are looking to reach a trade deal by the end of the year."We're making good progress in our trade negotiations with India. It is an exceptionally important relationship, on many, many levels. People-to-people levels, security levels and also trade and economic," Carney said."He (PM Modi) will be visiting Canada around that time. I very much look forward to hosting him," he added.This comes after Union commerce minister Piyush Goyal said that India and Canada have agreed to fast-track negotiations for a comprehensive economic partnership, with the next round of talks scheduled to begin on October 5.Goyal said he had concluded the fourth round of negotiations for the proposed trade agreement with his Canadian counterpart, minister of international trade Maninder Sidhu, in Mumbai last week."I have concluded the fourth round of negotiations for the Canada trade deal with my counterpart Mr Maninder Sidhu in Mumbai on Friday. Very productive discussions and both sides have resolved to fast-track negotiations, in view of which our team is now slated to go for the fifth round," he said."Fifth of October. So you can see that as the progress is taking shape, the speed of negotiations with Canada is also improving. Let's see, the next 90 days should be a very defining period in the Canada-India relationship," the minister said.India and Canada have discussed a comprehensive trade pact for more than a decade. Negotiations were formally relaunched in March 2022, with the two sides also pursuing an Early Progress Trade Agreement as an interim step. Nine negotiating rounds were held between 2022 and 2023 before the process was paused in August 2023 amid a period of strain in bilateral relations.Trade talks between India and Canada restarted during the G20 summit in 2025 as both countries saw a thaw in diplomatic relations post the standoff with former Canadian PM Justin Trudeau who had blamed India for the killing of designated terrorist Hardeep Nijjar in Canada.
Article Summary: Pm narendra modi is expected to visit canada in december to seal the trade deal. Canadian pm mark carney said that the relationship between india and canada is "exceptionally important" he claimed that both countries are looking to reach a trade deal by the end of the year.

Article Title: India teams up with EU, Canada & others to defend multilateralism; EAM says rules must be scrupulously followed
Article Text:
S Jaishankar At P4M Summit

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India joined the EU, Canada, Australia and several other countries in co-sponsoring a declaration expressing a joint commitment to multilateralism, international law, peace and prosperity, while expressing concern over escalating conflicts, trade disruption, power politics protectionism and coercion.The declaration followed the announcement of a new initiative titled Partners for Multilateralism (P4M) on the margins of the UN General Assembly that aims to make multilateral bodies more “representative, effective, legitimate and trusted” through middle-power cooperation, amid growing fragmentation and violations of international law.Drawing attention to geopolitical tensions, conflicts and extreme competition, foreign minister S Jaishankar said multilateralism will be best served when international law, rules, and norms are scrupulously observed.Other declaration co-sponsors included Brazil, Barbados and Kenya, making P4M a diverse group of countries that bridges – unlike the G7 and BRICS - the gap between the West and Global South. After the co-sponsors, 16 other countries signed off on the declaration that flagged increasing use of economic interdependence as a source of leverage, disrupting trade, supply chains, investment and development finance in messages directed at both US and China.The declaration stressed reform of multilateral institutions, including the UN, to promote fair trade, prevent conflicts and protect rule of law, while backing fair, open, resilient, predictable and inclusive economic cooperation, including more diversified and resilient global supply chains.The declaration said that the multilateral system founded on the UN Charter remained indispensable, as it had helped provide a framework for peace, decolonisation, prosperity, and human dignity. However, the declaration also said that it must now respond to a world that is more interconnected and complex, more contested and more multipolar.“We affirm the need to uphold and enforce the rules, principles and commitments that remain essential to international order, while renewing and reforming the multilateral system so that it is more effective, representative, inclusive and fit for purpose,” said the declaration, while stressing the joint commitment to sovereign equality, territorial integrity, peaceful settlement of disputes and prohibition of the threat or use of force.The inaugural meeting was co-hosted by European Council President Antonio Costa who said that the P4M will serve as a global network for dialogue, coalition-building and practical cooperation, helping us coordinate our response to shared challenges, with the UN at its core.As he underlined the need for multilateralism to assert itself strongly in these times, Jaishankar also pointed to the issue of terrorism. “The future of peace and international security, of climate action and climate justice, of emerging technologies and development finance ,of countering terrorism and strengthening supply chain, and of ensuring disaster resilience and preparing for pandemics, all depend on a will to cooperate,” he said.The minister also flagged the 4F crises of fuel, food, fertilizer and finance cannot be left to itself, saying where new capabilities and concerns arise, there is a very powerful case for frameworks and guardrails.“Where there is a threat of chokepoints dominance and disruption, de-risking and diversifying must be encouraged. And where there is a compelling cause or a powerful case, the like-minded must have the confidence to come together,” said Jaishankar, stressing the need for reformed multilateralism.
Article Summary: India joined the eu, canada, australia and several other countries in co-sponsoring a declaration. The declaration expressed a joint commitment to multilateralism, international law, peace and prosperity. It expressed concern over escalating conflicts, trade disruption, power politics protectionism and coercion.

Article Title: ‘Must act now’: Kashmiri leader urges UNHRC action over ‘worsening’ rights situation in PoJK, PoGB
Article Text:
Kashmiri urged the UNHRC to establish independent monitoring mechanisms for the two territories and seek accountability for alleged human rights violations.

Call for monitoring and accountability

Concerns over PoGB

United Kashmir People’s National Party (UKPNP) chairman Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri has urged the UN Human Rights Council (UNHRC) to take immediate action over what he described as a worsening human rights situation in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoJK) and Pakistan-occupied Gilgit-Baltistan (PoGB).Addressing the 63rd session of the UNHRC under Agenda Item 4, Kashmiri alleged that repression in PoJK had intensified since June 5, 2026. He cited reports of arrests, violence, deaths, injuries, alleged disappearances and restrictions on internet and mobile communications.Kashmiri called for an immediate, independent and impartial investigation into the reported violations. He also urged Pakistan to stop using force against peaceful protesters and release people he described as being arbitrarily detained."Peaceful dissent is not terrorism, and demanding rights is not a crime," Kashmiri said.Kashmiri urged the UNHRC to establish independent monitoring mechanisms for the two territories and seek accountability for alleged human rights violations He also called for the authorities to establish the whereabouts of missing persons and restore unrestricted internet and mobile communications across PoJK.The UKPNP chairman further called for the release of political prisoners in the Pakistan-occupied parts of Jammu and Kashmir.He said prolonged detention and alleged mistreatment should end."The Council must act now to safeguard the lives and fundamental rights of millions of Kashmiris," he said.On PoGB, Kashmiri raised concerns over political representation, land rights and control over natural resources. He called for genuine democratic dialogue to address the unresolved issues.He also said development projects in the region should be carried out transparently, with consultation and respect for local communities.Kashmiri concluded by urging the UNHRC to demand accountability and increase international scrutiny of the human rights situation in PoJK and PoGB.
Article Summary: Sardar shaukat ali kashmiri has urged the un human rights council (unhrc) to take immediate action over what he described as a worsening human rights situation in pakistan-occupied jammu and kashmir. Kashmiri alleged that repression in pojk had intensified since june 5, 2026.

Article Title: Pakistan must take credible action on crossborder terror before world believes it: MEA
Article Text:
India slams Pakistan over Permanent Court of Arbitration ruling

India seeks constructive ties with Bangladesh

275 Indians missing in Nepal

India reiterates dialogue, diplomacy on Ukraine

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Pakistan needs to take credible action against cross-border terrorism before the world can believe what it says, the ministry of external affairs said on Tuesday, while hitting out at Islamabad over its claims regarding a recent decision by the Permanent Court of Arbitration.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal accused Pakistan of “misrepresenting facts” and spreading “falsehoods” as part of its propaganda.“Pakistan has a habit of misrepresenting facts and propagating falsehoods to serve its malicious propaganda,” Jaiswal said.“For starters, the so-called ruling is not a ruling by the Permanent Court of Arbitration, as sought to be projected by the Pakistan minister. It is a ruling by an illegally constituted court. We see this as just one more attempt by Pakistan at distorting the reality,” he added.Jaiswal was responding to a question about Pakistan circulating a letter to the president of the UN Security Council regarding recent rulings related to the Permanent Court of Arbitration.His comments also came days after Pakistan increased the reward for information leading to the arrest or conviction of Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) chief Masood Azhar.India had last week described Pakistan's PKR 70 lakh reward for information on Azhar as a “phoney” move and asked Islamabad to take concrete action against the JeM chief.The Pakistan-based Jaish-e-Mohammed has been linked to several major terror attacks in India, including the 2001 Parliament attack and the attacks in Pathankot and Pulwama.The group was founded by most-wanted terrorist Masood Azhar.New Delhi has repeatedly called on Pakistan to take credible action against crossborder terrorism, saying Islamabad's actions would be a key test of the credibility of its claims.On India-Bangladesh relations, Jaiswal said New Delhi wants positive and constructive ties with Dhaka.“India seeks positive, constructive and forward-looking ties with Bangladesh,” he said.On Indians missing in Nepal floods, Jaiswal said an Indian forensic team was working with Nepalese authorities to identify those still unaccounted for.“As I told you last time, we had given you a figure of 275 Indian nationals who were missing. Over and above that, several other people from the Indian diaspora and persons of Indian origin are also missing,” he said.“We have a forensic team in Nepal that is working in Kathmandu in several laboratories along with their Nepali colleagues,” Jaiswal said.He said the Indian team was working on 3,000 samples and had so far arrived at more than 1,200 DNA profiles.“The work is going on, and regarding the missing Indian nationals and missing persons, we await to hear from the Nepali authorities,” he said.On the Ukraine conflict, Jaiswal said external affairs minister S Jaishankar met Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha on Monday and discussed recent developments.“Yes, the external affairs minister met with the Ukrainian foreign minister yesterday. During the meeting, he discussed the recent developments in the conflict,” Jaiswal said.Jaishankar reiterated India's position that dialogue and diplomacy are the way forward for a peaceful resolution.“The external affairs minister once again put forth India's point that dialogue and diplomacy are the way forward for a peaceful resolution,” Jaiswal said.“India, as you know, is in touch with both sides, Ukraine and Russia, and we have told them that if there is any way that India can contribute, India is ready to do so,” he added.
Article Summary: India slams pakistan over permanent court of arbitration ruling on cross-border terrorism. Mea spokesperson randhir jaiswal accused pakistan of “misrepresenting facts” and spreading “falsehoods” as part of its propaganda. India-bangladesh relations: india wants positive and constructive ties with dhaka.

Article Title: 4 European nations back India's bid for permanent UN seat, Jaishankar calls it 'historic'
Article Text:
Image credit: X/ Jaishankar

Jaishankar on V4's role in global affairs

Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and Czech Republic on Monday backed India's bid for a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council, with Slovakia foreign minister Juraj Blanár saying India, as a leading country of the Global South and an emerging power in the Indo-Pacific, should have a place at the UN's top decision-making body.The remarks came after external affairs minister S Jaishankar participated in the first high-level Visegrád Group (V4) plus India meeting on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York."We all agree, as V4 countries, that India, as part of the Global South, an upcoming superpower in the Indo-Pacific region, must be at the table as a permanent member of the UN Security Council," Blanár said.The V4 comprises Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia. The four countries held their first ministerial-level meeting with India in the new V4+India format during the UNGA high-level week.Jaishankar described the meeting as a "new historic occasion" and said the discussions covered political, economic, defence, technology, space, connectivity and people-to-people ties."We had our first Visegrad Four and India meeting. It was, in a sense, a new historic occasion, and I would like to thank Minister Juraj (Foreign Minister of Slovakia) for convening us today. It was a very, very productive meeting.What we agreed was that since India's relationship with the European Union itself is deepening, with the V4, we would take some special initiatives to create an annual business forum. As foreign ministers, we would meet annually. That was the consensus. We would also explore in technology and innovation whether we could be doing more. We have a very strong history with all the V4 countries in defense. We want to refresh and take forward that record and that cooperation. We discussed space issues, connectivity, and people-to-people mobility. We have students in each of the V4 countries. Overall, in terms of our cooperation, as well as a very good and useful exchange on the big global crisis, the Ukraine conflict, and what's happening in the Gulf. I think it was a very worthwhile and productive meeting. I'm very pleased about it."Asked about the political importance of the V4 for India on the global stage, Jaishankar said New Delhi viewed the four countries as partners with strong industrial, technological and innovation capabilities."We have very good relations with the V4 countries, and we know that these are countries with a very strong, very distinctive capability. They are industrial economies, economies with great innovation and technology talent. And I think how the V4 come together is for them to decide. But we certainly welcome the opportunity to work."India has been seeking reform of the UN Security Council and a permanent seat on the body. The Council currently has five permanent members, China, France, Russia, the UK and the US, alongside 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms.Jaishankar had formally launched India's campaign for a non-permanent UNSC term for 2028-29 in July, while New Delhi has continued to press for broader reform of the Council and permanent membership for India.Jaishankar said the meeting also resulted in an agreement to strengthen cooperation through annual foreign ministerial meetings and an annual business forum.In a post on X, Jaishankar said: "Our first meeting in the V4+India format agreed to: Closer political cooperation including annual meetings of Foreign Ministers. Deeper economic cooperation, including the Annual Business Forum. Reinvigorating our defence cooperation. Further development of our cultural cooperation and people-to-people relations."The meeting included Poland's deputy prime minister and foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, Hungary's deputy prime minister and foreign minister Dr Anita Orbán, Slovakia's foreign minister Juraj Blanár and Czechia's foreign minister Petr Macinka.Jaishankar is leading the Indian delegation at the 81st UN General Assembly high-level week in New York and is scheduled to address the General Debate on September 26.
Article Summary: Poland, hungary, slovakia and czech republic back india's bid for a permanent seat on the united nations security council. Slovakia foreign minister juraj blanár says india should have a place at the un's top decision-making body. Jaishankar is leading the indian delegation at the 81st un general assembly high-level week in new york.

Article Title: The Revisit: 125 shells, 10 minutes and a German attack on Madras - when WWI reached India
Article Text:
German cruiser SMS Emden that bombarded the city during the WWI on September 22.

The warship that did not look German

130 shells in one night

From harbour to high court

A city already preparing to flee

Why did Emden leave?

The word 'Emden' survives

The night war came home

When World War I broke out in Europe in July 1914, Madras was thousands of kilometres away from the battlefields. Yet there was little certainty among British authorities that the war would remain confined to Europe. The city's strategic importance as a major port made it vulnerable, and within weeks, residents were being advised to move towards safer places in the hinterland.By September, the anxiety had become real enough for some families to leave.Among them were the grandparents of PD Balaji, professor and head of the department of ancient history and archaeology at the University of Madras. Speaking to The Times of India in 2017 , Balaji recalled that his grandparents lived in Royapettah and moved to Salem briefly, taking some valuables with them because they feared Madras could come under attack.Their fears were realised on the night of September 22, 1914, when the German cruiser SMS Emden appeared off the Madras coast and opened fire.The attack lasted only a short time, but it became one of the most remarkable episodes of India's experience of World War I.The Emden had already been operating in the waters around the Indian subcontinent, attacking shipping before turning towards Madras. But the cruiser had an unusual advantage: it did not necessarily look like an enemy vessel from a distance.Historian Venkatesh Ramakrishnan told TOI that the Emden had a dummy fourth funnel, which made the German cruiser appear like a British ship.That deception was particularly useful in the busy waters of the region."Some enemy ships even saluted it during navigation," Ramakrishnan told TOI.The disguise allowed the cruiser to move through waters where a genuine German warship might otherwise have attracted immediate attention. By the time it approached Madras, the British authorities were facing a vessel that had managed to exploit both surprise and confusion.At around 9.30 pm, the attack began.The precise nature of the German target remains one of the interesting questions surrounding the bombardment. Some accounts have suggested that Fort St George was the intended target, while historian Venkatesh Ramakrishnan offered a different explanation.According to Ramakrishnan, Captain Karl von Müller did not necessarily direct his guns at one particular building."The Emden's captain Karl von Muller did not aim at any particular target. The shells were fired on any structure that was illuminated by the lighthouse," he told TOI.Around 130 shells were fired that night, according to Ramakrishnan.One struck a storage tank belonging to the Burmah Oil Company near the harbour. The tank caught fire, and the blaze continued for three days, turning the attack into a highly visible spectacle for the city.A separate 2014 TOI report, quoting historian V Dhivakar, put the number of shells at at least 125, fired within around 10 minutes. Dhivakar said the shells hit oil tanks containing approximately 350,000 gallons of oil.Whatever the precise count, the scale of the bombardment was remarkable for an attack that lasted only a short period.The German cruiser had sailed close enough to Madras to fire into the city and then withdrew before the British could mount an effective response.The attack was not confined to the waterfront.According to Ramakrishnan, shrapnel struck several parts of Madras, including the High Court, General Hospital, Vepery, Haddows Road, Poonamallee High Road, the gun battery at Royapuram, Casa Major Road and George Town.The geography of the damage is significant because it demonstrated how a naval attack on the harbour could quickly become a city-wide shock.For residents, the source of the explosions was initially not something they could easily understand. The war had until then existed largely in newspapers and official announcements. Suddenly, its sound could be heard across Madras.And the sight of the oil tank burning for days provided a lasting reminder that the British Empire's war had reached the Indian coast.The Emden attack did not come completely out of the blue.Anxiety had spread through Madras in the weeks following the outbreak of World War I. British authorities had advised residents to move to safer locations in the hinterland because of fears that enemy forces could attack the city.The exodus had already begun when the German cruiser struck.For families who had left, the decision suddenly appeared prescient. For those who remained, the bombardment reinforced fears that the Emden might return or that other German vessels could attack the city.The account of Balaji's grandparents provides a glimpse into what that uncertainty meant at an individual level. They left their Royapettah home for Salem and carried valuables with them, not knowing how long they would have to stay away.This was not merely a military episode. It had begun affecting ordinary civilian decisions.The attack also produced a question that historians continue to debate: Why did the Emden withdraw so quickly?The cruiser had managed to reach Madras, fire more than a hundred shells and hit important infrastructure. Yet it did not remain to inflict prolonged damage.Historian V Dhivakar challenged the later British explanation that Emden withdrew because of the British response.“After Emden reached a safe distance, the British started responding towards what for them was an unknown object in the dark far out at sea,” Dhivakar told TOI.He argued that the German cruiser could potentially have inflicted considerably more damage had it remained longer.The question becomes more intriguing when the Emden's capabilities are considered. Dhivakar described the cruiser as a formidable warship for its time, armed with ten 10.5cm guns and two torpedo tubes.Why Muller chose to stop when he did remains one of the enduring mysteries of the Madras raid.The Emden story also acquired an Indian revolutionary dimension through Chempakaraman Pillai, an Indian-born political activist and revolutionary who was living in Germany.A persistent claim has suggested that Pillai helped the Germans plan the Madras attack or was aboard the Emden.But the evidence cited by Dhivakar does not establish that.He told TOI that Pillai was not aboard the Emden during its wartime operations. Dhivakar referred to a book by Hellmuth von Mucke, the ship's vice-commander, which recorded several incidents aboard the cruiser without mentioning Pillai.Mucke did, however, refer to an Indian passenger who provided information.That detail has helped keep the Indian connection alive, but it does not prove that Pillai himself was involved in the attack.The most curious legacy of the raid may have been linguistic.The name Emden became part of popular usage in southern India, particularly in Tamil, where it came to be associated with someone formidable, daring or intimidating.The German cruiser therefore outlived its own military career in an unexpected way.The ship was eventually cornered and destroyed later in 1914, but its name had already acquired a place in Indian memory.For Madras, meanwhile, the physical reminders of the bombardment became part of the city's history. The High Court was among the places struck by shrapnel, while accounts of the attack have continued to document the damage caused across the harbour and surrounding neighbourhoods.The Emden attack did not change the outcome of World War I. It did not result in the capture of Madras, nor did it lead to a prolonged German campaign on the Indian coast.Its significance was different.It showed that a war that seemed distant and European could reach an Indian city with little warning. It exposed the vulnerability of a major colonial port, sent residents fleeing towards the interior and forced the British to confront the possibility that India's coastline could become part of the global conflict.For the people of Madras, September 22, 1914, was therefore not simply another date in the history of World War I.It was the night when the distant war suddenly became local: when a German cruiser appeared off the coast, 130 shells tore into the city, a Burmah Oil tank burned for three days, shrapnel reached the High Court and other parts of Madras, and a word that once belonged to a German warship entered the vocabulary of southern India.
Article Summary: German cruiser sms emden opened fire on madras on september 22, 1914. Around 130 shells were fired that night, according to historian venkatesh ramakrishnan. Shrapnel struck several parts of madras, including the high court, general hospital, and gun battery. The emden attack did not come completely out of the blue.

Article Title: Critical thinking: Don’t just know. Know how to think
Article Text:
Educators say initiatives like Times Critical Thinking Championship can encourage inquiry-driven learning and help move schools beyond rote memorisation

Can you crack these?

Sample questions that tested how students think

A massive meteorite crashes into the Moon, causing a huge explosion. How many seconds later will an astronaut 1,000km away hear the blast?

Never, as sound cannot travel through the vacuum of space.People living then could not have used the term “BC”, or “Before Christ”.Both land simultaneously because there is no air resistance.None. Half a dozen means six.Kabir.What makes someone a critical thinker? The ability to question an accepted assumption, decide with incomplete information, diagnose why a machine has gone wrong, or simply have the confidence to say, “I may be wrong”? From classrooms and boardrooms to battlefields and AI, eight experts brought very different answers to that question at the AM/NS India Times Critical Thinking Championship 2026, an initiative conceived and conducted by Times Foundation.And increasingly, they argued, the challenge is not access to answers but what we do with them. AI can produce information and arguments within seconds, but outsourcing judgement to it can weaken rather than strengthen thinking. Knowledge, curiosity and the ability to ask the right question remain essential to evaluating whatever answer technology provides.The discussion on ‘Critical Thinking, Pedagogy, Practice & Policy’ explored how AI could sharpen rather than weaken young minds. Panellists examined the role of curiosity in classrooms, independent decision-making at work and the challenge of training teachers, many themselves brought up on rote learning, to nurture questioning students.Setting out the risks of unquestioning dependence on technology, Ira Singhal, deputy secretary, department of school education and literacy, education ministry, spoke of her niece, who used AI to solve maths problems but returned with incorrect answers and no working steps. “AI is an amazing tool only when you know the subject and possess the basic knowledge needed to use it. Most assume they do not need knowledge because AI has it, and that is where the problem begins,” she said.The need to question established assumptions, panellists said, extended well beyond the use of AI. Ruchi Ghanshyam, (retd) IFS, former High Commissioner of India to the UK, explained how such questioning could turn routine administration into meaningful action. While the instinctive bureaucratic response was often “Why should this be done?”, she said she learnt to reverse the question. “I learnt to ask, ‘Why not?’ If something is good, why shouldn’t we do it? That takes us to the more difficult question of how it can be done,” she said. Merely moving a file from the ‘in’ to the ‘out’ tray achieved little, she added. “Between the in-tray and the out-tray is a human mind.”Returning to the role of technology in learning, former Delhi University vice-chancellor Professor Dinesh Singh urged students not to fear AI but engage with it intelligently and inquisitively. “Do not engage with AI mechanically. Be inquisitive, keep asking questions and, most importantly, do not be afraid to admit that you do not know something. Learn to say, ‘I don’t know, tell me’, and you can learn a great deal from AI,” he said. AI was advancing rapidly and would not disappear, he added, making it essential for teachers and students to know its capabilities.Taking the discussion deeper into the origins of independent thought, Gurcharan Das, thought leader and former CEO, Procter & Gamble India, placed curiosity at the heart of critical thinking. He contrasted adults cautiously walking around a puddle with a child jumping into it simply to discover what it felt like. “Critical thinking does not begin with intelligence, but with wonder. Wonder leads to question, question to doubt, doubt to evidence, evidence to judgement and judgement, ultimately, to independence of mind,” he said. That natural instinct to explore, Das said, was often weakened rather than encouraged in classrooms. He warned that education systems frequently suppress curiosity by rewarding repetition over inquiry.Rote learning, he said, created “a nation of parrots”, while students needed confidence to question teachers and authority.The discussion also located these ideas within India’s own intellectual history. Professor Shailendra Mehta, former president and director, MICA, Ahmedabad, traced critical thinking to the Sanskrit concept of Anvikshiki, which he described as the process of examining and interpreting what one observes. Referring to Chanakya’s mentorship of Chandragupta Maurya, he said Anvikshiki was regarded as the foundation of learning, action and right conduct. “For thousands of years, we have understood that critical thinking is what can make a pauper a prince,” he said.From intellectual traditions, the conversation moved to situations in which independent judgement could carry serious consequences. Maj Gen K Narayanan of NITI Aayog said critical thinking in the armed forces involved analysing information without becoming trapped in “paralysis by analysis”. At the operational level, personnel often had to act amid incomplete information and serious consequences. “The person on the ground cannot always look for orders. Decisions have to be taken in the absence of complete facts and amid the fog of war,” he said, describing the process through the cycle of observing, orienting, deciding and acting.A similar need for clear judgement arose in organisational leadership, particularly when decisions had to be taken under pressure. Deepak Kapoor, former chairman, PwC India, said, “Critical thinking was inseparable from effective leadership, particularly during a crisis, when organisations could become defensive or slip into denial. Leaders needed to set aside biases, keep alternatives open and give colleagues the freedom to question decisions without fear or internal politics. ” The same ability, he said, was required while using AI, as its usefulness depended on intelligent prompts, scrutiny of biases and consideration of multiple perspectives.At the level of everyday work, critical thinking was presented not as an abstract idea but an essential part of applying knowledge. Sandeep Achantani, director, NAMTECH School of Technical Education, linked it with vocational skills, noting that real-world problems rarely arrived with all the variables marked out. A machine operator diagnosing faulty output or a mechanic tracing a glitch must test several possible causes before finding a solution. “Knowledge lays the foundation, but critical thinking converts that knowledge into skill and that skill into good professional practice,” he said.Together, these examples brought the discussion back to the classroom and the environments in which young people form their habits of thought. The conversation also extended to how constant exposure to information is shaping the way young people think and make judgements.Ashutosh Telang, director and vice-president, HR and administration, AM/NS India, said: “Use technology and AI, and learn from them, but do not outsource your judgement. Technology should augment your thinking, not replace it. Listen to those who disagree, remain open to better evidence and use your thinking to solve problems.”Impact catalyst Aruna Goenka; Pushpendra Rajput, former Secretary, UPSC; and Vikas Yadvendu, head of CSR, AM/NS India, were also present at the event.The stress on questioning was highlighted by other guests, too. Chief guest Sanjay Kumar, who was, till recently, secretary, department of school education & literacy, education ministry, said: “What children learn, how they learn and how they question depend largely on how they are assessed. Assessment patterns must change, and classroom interactions must become two-way, with every child encouraged to ask questions and participate in conversations. ”Extending the message from the classroom to life, guest of honour Lt Gen Sanjay Kulkarni (retd), former director general of infantry, Indian Army, said: “Do not be afraid to fail or ask questions. Accept failure as a challenge, identify what was lacking and improve. Knowledge and hard work matter, but attitude makes the difference. Develop a positive attitude, learn to say ‘yes’ and find a solution.”
Article Summary: Educators say initiatives like times critical thinking championship can encourage inquiry-driven learning. Panellists examined the role of curiosity in classrooms, independent decision-making at work and the challenge of training teachers to nurture questioning students.

Article Title: ‘Global order under stress’: Jaishankar calls for stronger multilateralism at UNGA
Article Text:
EAM S Jaishankar during P4M Summit

External affairs minister S Jaishankar called for stronger multilateralism to navigate rising geopolitical tensions, conflicts and global competition, as he co-chaired the first Partners for Multilateralism, International Law, Peace & Prosperity (P4M) Summit with European Council President Antonio Costa on Monday (local time). The summit was held on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York.Minister Jaishankar stressed the need for greater international cooperation and called for steps to address ongoing conflicts, create safeguards for emerging technologies and reduce risks linked to dominance and disruption. He also stressed the importance of international law, rules and norms.In a post on X, Jaishankar said the summit provided an opportunity to underline the importance of multilateralism at a time when international cooperation is facing pressure from intense competition, geopolitical tensions and conflicts.He highlighted the need to address the specific dimensions of ongoing conflicts, establish frameworks and safeguards for emerging capabilities, and reduce risks by diversifying against dominance and disruption. He also underlined the importance of international law, rules and norms.The EAM further called for “reformed multilateralism”, saying more participative discussions and transparent decision-making could help restore hope in the UN system and strengthen countries’ resolve to work together.Addressing the summit, Jaishankar thanked European Council President Antonio Costa for initiating the forum and said India was pleased to join as a co-sponsor. He said the global order was under stress, with a long-running rebalancing of the world taking a different shape amid intensifying competition, geopolitical tensions and conflicts.He said that if these pressures were left unchecked, they could undermine the spirit of international cooperation, making it crucial for multilateralism to assert itself more strongly."We meet at a time when the global order is under stress. For some decades, the world has witnessed a steady rebalancing, which was a long-expected structural evolution. However, extreme competition, geopolitical tensions, and actual conflicts have given this an entirely different character. If left unchecked, it would call into question the very spirit of international cooperation. That is why it is so essential that multilateralism asserts itself strongly at this juncture. "Jaishankar also highlighted the range of issues that he said depended on countries' willingness to cooperate, including peace and international security, climate action and climate justice, emerging technologies, development finance, countering terrorism, strengthening supply chains, disaster resilience and pandemic preparedness."At stake here are very real issues, not just words and expressions. The future of peace and international security, of climate action and climate justice, of emerging technologies and development finance, of countering terrorism and strengthening supply chains, and of ensuring disaster resilience and preparing for pandemics. All depend on a will to cooperate."The summit also saw Jaishankar make a case for Reformed Multilateralism, with participative deliberations and transparent decision-making being highlighted as ways to provide hope and optimism to the UN system and reinforce countries' resolve to work together.Meanwhile, Slovakia backed India's bid for a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council on Monday, with foreign minister Juraj Blanár saying India, as a leading country of the Global South and an emerging power in the Indo-Pacific, should have a place at the UN's top decision-making body.Blanar's remarks came after Jaishankar participated in the first high-level Visegrád Group (V4) plus India meeting on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York."We all agree, as V4 countries, that India, as part of the Global South, an upcoming superpower in the Indo-Pacific region, must be at the table as a permanent member of the UN Security Council," Blanár said.The V4 comprises Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia. The four countries held their first ministerial-level meeting with India in the new V4+India format during the UNGA high-level week.Jaishankar described the meeting as a "new historic occasion". Discussions covered political, economic, defence, technology, space, connectivity and people-to-people ties.Jaishankar is leading the Indian delegation at the 81st UN General Assembly high-level week in New York and is scheduled to address the General Debate on September 26.
Article Summary: Eam s jaishankar called for stronger multilateralism to navigate rising geopolitical tensions, conflicts and global competition. He co-chaired the first partners for multilateralism, international law, peace & prosperity summit with european council president antonio costa.

Article Title: WHO puts stroke, cancer, mental health on 10-year traditional medicine research agenda
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: From stroke and cancer to mental health and pain management, the World Health Organization has identified major health conditions for research into traditional, complementary and integrative medicine over the next decade.Its 2025-2034 research agenda identifies stroke, mental health, pain management, musculoskeletal conditions, cancer, metabolic and endocrine disorders, and reproductive health and childbirth as priority areas. Prevention and health promotion, healthy ageing and healthy childhood are also included.The report highlights a striking mismatch between disease burden and research. Stroke ranks third globally in causes of mortality and disability, yet less than 1% of traditional, complementary and integrative medicine-funded grants address the condition. Mental health ranks eighth among contributors to disability-adjusted life years, but the review found very few or no grants specifically focused on mental health conditions. Musculoskeletal conditions are also a prominent cause of disability globally but remain under-researched relative to their burden.Cancer, too, features among the priority areas, with the report noting rising global incidence and calling for research into integrative oncology and palliative care.For metabolic health and endocrine disorders, WHO identifies the need for stronger evidence, including longer-term studies on conditions such as type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome.WHO says the aim is to generate stronger evidence on effectiveness, safety, regulation and health-system integration so countries can make informed decisions about the role of these approaches in healthcareThe research agenda also puts patient safety under the spotlight. It calls for studies on herb-drug interactions, monitoring and reporting of adverse events, regulatory and quality-assurance systems, and the safe integration of traditional, complementary and integrative medicine into primary healthcare.The push comes against a broader funding gap. WHO says traditional, complementary and integrative medicine is widely used globally, with use reaching up to 80% of populations in some settings, while less than 1% of global health research funding is directed towards research in the field.India has a direct connection to the agenda. The WHO report acknowledges financial support from the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India, for its development and publication. India was also among the health ministries that participated in the Second WHO Global Summit on Traditional Medicine, held in New Delhi in December 2025.The report, however, is a research-prioritisation framework rather than a clinical guideline or recommendation to use any particular traditional medicine.
Article Summary: World health organization identifies major health conditions for research into traditional, complementary and integrative medicine. 2025-2034 research agenda identifies stroke, mental health, pain management, musculoskeletal conditions, cancer, metabolic and endocrine disorders.

Article Title: 'No burden for consumers': Sitharaman clarifies who will pay MDR on UPI transactions
Article Text:
Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman

Union finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman has backed the recently announced Merchant Discount Rate (MDR), saying that the mechanism will be imposed on operators and will not be passed on to customers. Addressing ongoing speculations around the charges, FM blamed the opposition for creating confusion and urged people to remain alert.Speaking to ANI, the finance minister said that she had already addressed the issue in Parliament, stressing that MDR is a charge between payment operators and will not be 'burdened' on UPI users.Sitharaman stressed that MDR is neither a tax nor a cess and that the money collected through it will not go into the Consolidated Fund of India.”It does not apply to transactions below Rs 2,000. It is neither a tax nor a cess; the funds will not be deposited into the Consolidated Fund of India. It is a charge levied by service providers to improve the system and provide better service, not for small transactions. Moreover, it is a charge between operators; it will not be passed on to the consumer. The burden does not fall on the customer,” she said.Sitharaman said she had given the same clarification earlier too, when the issue came up during the parliamentary session.“I provided a clarification on this very point when the issue was raised during the parliamentary session. Spreading misinformation, fueling debates based on it, and using that narrative to attack the government has become a habit for the opposition. This is wrong; there is an effort to spread misconceptions and mislead the public. The public needs to remain vigilant," Sitharaman added.Meanwhile, Niti Aayog NITI Aayog vice chairman Ashok Kumar Lahiri had also backed the Centre’s decision to introduce a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on high-value UPI transactions, saying that businesses should find ways to sustain themselves instead of relying on government subsidies.Lahiri drew on the words of ancient philosopher Chanakya to make his point, saying a ruler should collect taxes from citizens as a bee collects honey from a flower — “gently, gradually, and without inflicting pain or bruising the petals”.“So you have to find ways of sustaining businesses without having to give subsidy,” Lahiri told reporters on the sidelines of an event.He clarified that the view was his personal opinion and did not represent NITI Aayog’s official position.The government has ruled out any rethink on the decision, with a senior official telling PTI, “There is no question of a re-think.”FM Sitharaman’s clarification comes after the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) introduced a new MDR framework on September 15. Under the framework, an MDR of 0.4 per cent will apply to Person-to-Merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above Rs 2,000, subject to a cap of Rs 300 per transaction.Consumers will continue to transact free of cost using UPI. The government has said that around 96 per cent of P2M transactions will remain unaffected, while the MDR will be distributed among payment ecosystem participants, including banks and payment application providers.
Article Summary: Finance minister nirmala sitharaman has backed the recently announced merchant discount rate (mdr) she stressed that mdr is neither a tax nor a cess and that the money collected through it will not go into the consolidated fund of india. Fm blamed the opposition for creating confusion and urged people to remain alert.

Article Title: Kushner, Witkoff meet Iran mediators for over 3 hours: All you need to know
Article Text:
Kushner, Witkoff hold 3-hour meeting with Iran mediators amid Trump’s threats

Who was involved in the meeting?

Trump had threatened to ‘annihilate’ Iran

What Trump said about the possible deal

What happens next?

US President Donald Trump said US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were part of the American team that met with Iranian officials and mediators in New York, with the talks lasting around three hours as Washington and Tehran face renewed pressure to reach an agreement.Trump described the meeting as a "very good meeting" but provided few details about who represented Iran or what was discussed. The talks came shortly after Trump warned in his address to the United Nations General Assembly that he could "annihilate" Iran if an agreement was not reached.Speaking during his bilateral meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Trump said, "The meeting went very well. It ended an hour ago. It was a meeting that lasted for three hours...It was a very good meeting..."Trump later said the Iranian officials involved were "not the highest level, but it's something", according to AP.Trump said Witkoff and Kushner met with mediators involved in efforts to reach a deal with Iran."Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with the mediators on the Iran deal. The mediators were here...A lot of things are working out very well," Trump said.The engagement came amid renewed diplomatic activity around the UN General Assembly in New York. Earlier on Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump was open to meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during the gathering, although he said such engagement would depend on whether it could produce a constructive outcome.US and Iranian communications had previously taken place through mediators, including Qatar and Pakistan. The latest meeting marks another attempt to keep diplomatic channels open despite the continuing conflict between Washington and Tehran.The meeting took place just hours after Trump's address to the UN General Assembly, where he said he faced a choice between reaching a deal with Iran and taking further military action."I have a big decision to make," Trump said. "Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world. Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?"Trump also called on Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and return to negotiations. Reuters reported that his UN speech combined threats of further action with indications that a diplomatic agreement could still be possible.Trump suggested that Iran had a choice between further conflict and an agreement that could allow the country to rebuild."I can't imagine why they wouldn't want to do it... In one case, it's obliteration and the other alternative is potential greatness. It could be a great country,” he said.Trump has previously said that preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons remains a central objective of US policy. Rubio also said earlier Tuesday that any potential engagement would need to address that issue.The meeting does not by itself indicate that a deal has been reached. Trump described the talks positively but did not announce an agreement or provide details of the issues discussed.Trump also met with leaders and senior officials from Gulf Cooperation Council countries and Jordan on Tuesday to discuss the Iran conflict, while the UN General Assembly provided an opportunity for multiple diplomatic contacts around the war.The latest engagement comes as the conflict continues to affect regional security and global energy markets, particularly because of the importance of the Strait of Hormuz to international oil and gas shipments.
Article Summary: Kushner, witkoff hold 3-hour meeting with iran mediators amid trump’s threats. Trump described the meeting as a "very good meeting" but provided few details about who represented iran or what was discussed. The talks came shortly after trump warned in his address to the united nations general assembly that he could "annihilate" iran if an agreement was not reached.

Article Title: Russian oligarch’s wedding gift to Trump Jr puts family dealings under scrutiny
Article Text:
Russian oligarch’s wedding gift for Trump Jr puts family dealings under scrutiny

Curtis seeks scrutiny of Jr's foreign ties

Russian oligarch helped fund wedding celebrations

More facts needed

A Russian oligarch’s role in Donald Trump Jr’s wedding celebrations has now sparked a call for a Senate investigation from the GOP. Republican senator John Curtis of Utah has asked the Judiciary Committee to examine whether US president Donald Trump’s son benefited financially from his proximity to the White House.Curtis, who is not a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, made the request in a letter sent on Tuesday to committee chairman Chuck Grassley, a Republican from Iowa, and the panel’s top Democrat, Illinois Senator Dick Durbin. He asked the committee to subpoena Trump Jr over his business dealings, relationships with foreign individuals and entities, gifts and other benefits he has received, and any instances in which his relationship with President Donald Trump “was invoked or understood to provide value. ”Curtis also called for the same scrutiny of Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden.“The country should not have to accept one standard for the family of a Republican president and another for the family of a Democratic president,” Curtis wrote.The request puts a Republican senator at the centre of scrutiny of Trump’s family at a time when most Republican lawmakers have largely avoided weighing in on the president’s son.Curtis, who was first elected to the Senate in 2024, has previously vowed not to shy away from disagreements with Trump. He has publicly broken with the president several times, including rejecting Trump’s calls to eliminate the Senate filibuster.His latest criticism, however, goes beyond a disagreement over policy. Curtis last Friday described the reported wedding funding as “corruption” and said he would say more about the issue in the coming days.“A Russian oligarch paid for a lavish wedding after-party for Donald Trump Jr, which to me just stinks. It’s corruption. I don’t like it,” Curtis said in a video posted on social media.Earlier on Tuesday, Curtis also referred to the Republican-led scrutiny of Hunter Biden’s foreign relationships, writing that Republicans “nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden’s foreign relationships” and that they “should not unplug it now.”The controversy follows a report by ProPublica last week that Umar Kremlev, who has close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin, helped pay for the rental of a private island and a fireworks show during celebrations for Trump Jr and socialite Bettina Anderson’s wedding in the Bahamas in May.Bettina Trump later addressed Kremlev’s involvement in an Instagram post signed by the couple. She described Kremlev, who is head of the International Boxing Association, as a “dear friend” who “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding.”Though Trump did not attend his son’s wedding, he defended Kremlev’s involvement but said the money would be paid back.Curtis’ letter asks the Judiciary Committee to examine Trump Jr’s business dealings, his relationships with foreign individuals and entities, and gifts or other benefits he has received. It also seeks scrutiny of instances in which his relationship with the president “was invoked or understood to provide value.”Grassley has not yet committed to an investigation. Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, he said he was not yet familiar with the facts surrounding the case and would need to gather more information before deciding what action to take.“I’m going to take these requests seriously and sit down with staff and see what we can do,” Grassley said.He added that the process would take time and said, “it takes time, and if you were going to ask me when we're going to have a hearing, there’s no way I could answer that today.”Senate majority leader John Thune, Republican of South Dakota, also declined to offer a view, saying he did not “have an observation on that.”Still, some Republican lawmakers have indicated that they would support Curtis’ request.The developments come as a few Republicans have recently shown a greater willingness to criticise Trump’s policies after largely avoiding public breaks with him during much of his second term.Meanwhile, the ongoing war in Iran, high gas prices and mounting concerns about Republican prospects in November’s midterm elections have brought increased scrutiny of the president from within his own party.
Article Summary: Republican senator john curtis of utah has asked the judiciary committee to examine whether us president donald trump’s son benefited financially from his proximity to the white house. Umar kremlev, who has close ties to russian president vladimir putin, helped pay for the rental of a private island and a fireworks show during celebrations for trump jr. grassley said he was not yet familiar with the facts surrounding the case.

Article Title: Indian Navy plans to procure six more landing craft utility platforms to boost amphibious operations
Article Text:
Indian Navy plans to procure six LCU Mk V vessels to boost amphibious, logistics and HADR capabilities.

NEW DELHI: To strengthen its amphibious operations, logistics and HADR capabilities, the Indian Navy is planning to procure six landing craft utility (LCU) MK V from Indian shipyards as it has issued a request for information (RFI) for six such platforms.A Landing Craft Utility (LCU) is a rugged, steel-hulled watercraft used by amphibious forces to transport heavy equipment, vehicles, and troops from ship to shore, along a coast, or back to warships. They are also used for humanitarian assistance and disaster relief, medical evacuation and specialized maritime operations.The Indian Navy currently has 8 active Landing Craft Utility (LCU) ships, all belonging to the indigenous Mk IV class. These amphibious ships displace about 830 tonnes and are primarily stationed under the Andaman and Nicobar Command for beaching, transport, and humanitarian missions. They can transport Main Battle Tanks (like Arjun or T-72), armoured vehicles, and up to 160 troops.According to the RFI, “The procurement of the vessel will be as per Defence Procurement Procedure 2.0, and accordingly shipyards are required to submit the details regarding indigenous content.The categorisation for the procurement is intended to be under Buy (Indian - IDDM).”Such a vessel with a displacement of 1,500 tonnes should be capable of carrying at least four main battle tanks (MBTs), 4 BMP infantry combat vehicles, and 190 troops and should have maximum speed of 15 knots or more with an endurance of around 4,500 nautical miles.“Shipyards may consider this RFI as advance information to obtain requisite govt clearances and setting up of necessary infrastructure both in terms of manpower and material requirements,” it said .
Article Summary: Indian navy plans to procure six lcu mk v vessels to boost amphibious, logistics and hadr capabilities. Landing craft utility (lcu) is a rugged, steel-hulled watercraft used by amphibious forces to transport heavy equipment, vehicles, and troops from ship to shore.

Article Title: Peacemaker with a warning to annihilate: The major contradictions in Trump's UN speech
Article Text:
Donald Trump used much of his address at the UN to list his achievements. (AP photo)

Peacemaker to annihilator

US President Donald Trump returned to the United Nations podium Tuesday wearing two very different hats. One moment he was the global peacemaker who had "ended eight wars", the next he was threatening to wipe out Iran.The gap between these two versions captures the uncertain order Trump has built, or perhaps enabled, during his second term in the White House.Trump used much of his address to the General Debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly to list his achievements, much as he did a year ago when he cast himself as the standout contender for the Nobel Peace Prize. This year, though, the prize went unmentioned. Instead, his tone hardened, with attacks on the International Criminal Court (ICC), the UN's climate agenda and Unesco.Trump also pointed to his effort to launch a "Board of Peace" in January, which appeared another swipe at the UN, with him at one point suggesting his new creation might end up replacing it.Ironically, within a month of the board's creation, the US and Israel launched a joint military operation against Iran, one that has continued in some form since."Since I took office, it has been my great honour to settle eight wars, and in so doing, become friendly with the leaders of many of those countries.It was a great honour to do it. Numerous of these wars have gone on for many years and even decades," he told the assembled leaders.He credited his success to what he called "very special relationships", along with the use and threat of tariffs.Among the conflicts he claimed to have resolved were the disputes between Cambodia and Thailand, Kosovo and Serbia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda, Pakistan and India, and Armenia and Azerbaijan, as well as the war in Gaza.He repeated a claim India has long rejected, that he brokered peace between India and Pakistan last year."The Prime Minister of Pakistan, terrific man, said that Donald Trump was responsible for saving 30 million lives and probably many more than that," Trump said.India has always maintained the ceasefire came from direct talks between the two countries' military operations chiefs, with Pakistani DGMO seeking the truce amid Operation Sindoor.He also mentioned Russia and Ukraine, saying his team is "working very closely" with both sides. "We will get that one done. It's going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand," he said.Having spent much of the speech basking in the image of a dealmaker, Trump turned to Iran, warning that Tehran must either negotiate with Washington or face destruction.Iran would never be allowed to have nuclear weapons, he said, adding that he faces "a big decision to make.""Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?"He went further still, asking, "Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?" He then predicted a deal was more likely once the midterm elections were over, since Iran was "waiting to see how I do in the midterm election," despite Trump not being on the ballot himself.Lo and behold, Trump's speech offered a portrait of a President who saw no contradiction in claiming the mantle of peacemaker while reserving the language of annihilation for those who resist his terms.
Article Summary: Trump used much of his address to the general debate of the 81st session of the un general assembly to list his achievements. This year, though, the prize went unmentioned. Instead, his tone hardened, with attacks on the international criminal court (icc), the un's climate agenda and unesco.

Article Title: Donald Trump wants to rename AI; says: 'artificial' makes AI sound fake, renames it 'super intelligence'; It is exactly the opposite of...
Article Text:
Trump picked 'super intelligence' after two social media polls

US president says whoever wins super intelligence wins the world

Superintelligence already has a very different meaning in AI research

US President Donald Trump wants the world to stop saying "artificial intelligence". Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday (September 22), Trump said the US will now officially call the technology "super intelligence", or SI. His reason is simple: the word "artificial" makes it sound fake. "It makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It's actually amazing," he said.The change, according to Trump, will cover all US government documents. "From this point forward, all of the United States documents, and hopefully the world's, will be changed to use the much more accurate term, super as opposed to artificial," he told the assembly. There is no word yet on when the switch will happen or how it will be carried out. Trump himself did not sound too sure. "Let's see if I have any power. Maybe I do, and maybe I don't, we're gonna find out pretty soon," he said.The idea did not come out of nowhere. On Saturday (September 19), Trump posted on X and Truth Social that "many people think that the words 'Artificial Intelligence' are inaccurate, and very ineloquent." He then asked followers to vote on three options: Superior Intelligence, Extreme Intelligence and Supreme Intelligence."Superior Intelligence" took an early lead with around 39% of the vote and later crossed 41%. Then, on Monday, Trump ran a second poll that pitted "Superior Intelligence" against a new entry, "Super Intelligence". The new option won comfortably, and Trump started using "SI" in his posts almost immediately. So the name he announced at the UN was not even on the original ballot.The same weekend, Trump said he was forming an "AI Force", modelled on the Space Force from his first term. He also promised to name an AI czar soon, adding, "Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" He did not explain what either would do.At the UN, the rename came wrapped in a larger message about the AI race. "Whoever wins super intelligence wins," Trump said, adding that the US is "leading now over China by a lot."He was clear that his government will not slow the technology down. "I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution," he said. He added that the Department of Justice and other law enforcement bodies would "watch it closely" and step in if needed. In the same breath, he argued that the fear around AI gets it wrong. "In fact, it is exactly the opposite of what it purports," he said.Trump also lumped AI safety warnings with climate change and the "Russia, Russia, Russia hoax". Earlier in the week, he had called the backlash against AI a hoax pushed by his political rivals. The comments come after an Anthropic researcher resigned, saying leading AI companies believe the technology "could kill us all by the end of the decade." Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has since proposed a plan to "pace the frontier", which OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk appeared to back.There is a catch with Trump's pick. In AI circles, "superintelligence" is not a new word. Philosopher Nick Bostrom described it back in 1997 as "an intellect that is much smarter than the best human brains in practically every field." Researchers use it for hypothetical future systems that outperform humans across most tasks. Today's chatbots are not there yet, and Bostrom's work is largely about the risks such systems could pose."Artificial intelligence" itself has no legal status that a president can overwrite. Computer scientist John McCarthy coined it in a 1955 proposal for a Dartmouth College conference, co-authored with Claude Shannon, Marvin Minsky and Nathaniel Rochester. At the time, rival labels such as "automata studies" and "complex information processing" were also doing the rounds. "AI" won, and it has stuck for 70 years. It is even part of company names like OpenAI.Trump has renamed things before. The Gulf of Mexico and Denali got new labels, and digital maps in the US updated within days. A word used by millions of engineers, companies and users every day is a different test. Government files may say SI soon. Whether anyone outside Washington follows is the part Trump admitted he cannot predict.
Article Summary: Us president says whoever wins super intelligence wins the world. Trump picked'super intelligence' after two social media polls on saturday and monday. In ai circles, "superintelligence" is not a new word. Researchers use it for hypothetical future systems that outperform humans.

Article Title: Iran war risk: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns of oil shocks, sticky inflation and higher interest rates
Article Text: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that the ongoing war in Iran could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated and pushing interest rates higher than current market expectations, Reuters reported.The warning came in his annual letter to shareholders, a day after US President Donald Trump escalated pressure on Iran by threatening to target key infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened."Now, because of the war in Iran, we additionally face the potential for significant ongoing oil and commodity price shocks, along with the reshaping of global supply chains, which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect," Dimon said, news agency Reuters quoted as saying.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan for two decades, also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China."The challenges we all face are significant," he added.He said it remains uncertain whether the Iran war will achieve US objectives, while warning that nuclear proliferation remains the biggest risk linked to Iran.Markets have already begun pricing in these risks, with expectations of interest rate cuts this year largely fading amid rising inflation concerns triggered by the conflict.Last week, the benchmark S&P 500 index recorded its worst quarterly performance since 2022, weighed down by rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty since late February.Dimon noted that the US economy remains resilient, with consumers continuing to earn and spend, and businesses staying broadly healthy, though signs of weakening have emerged.He cautioned that economic strength has been supported by significant government deficit spending and past stimulus, while infrastructure investment needs continue to grow.At the same time, he pointed to positives such as fiscal stimulus under President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill", deregulation policies and rising capital expenditure driven by artificial intelligence.On financial stability, Dimon said the $1.8-trillion private credit market "probably" does not pose a systemic risk, despite investor concerns and recent withdrawals from such funds.However, he warned that in a downturn, losses across leveraged lending could exceed expectations as credit standards have weakened.Private credit markets also lack transparency and rigorous valuation benchmarks, increasing the risk of investor exits if conditions worsen, he said.Separately, Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical" and "very flawed".He said JPMorgan’s GSIB surcharge would fall only to 5.0%, a level he described as “absurd” and “un-American”, arguing it penalises the bank’s scale and performance.
Article Summary: Jpmorgan chase ceo jamie dimon warns iran war could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated. He also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in ukraine, tensions in the middle east and friction with china. Dimon criticised revised us capital rules, including basel iii and gsib surcharge norms.
